name: Cocos (Keeling) Islands
territory: Australia (external territory, administered by the Australian Government)

creatures.iucn_status: Endangered (EN), criteria A2bcd; assessment 17 July 2024 per FishBase (Wikipedia cites a 2004 assessment)
creatures.status_note: Presence verified via GBIF (24 Cocos records) and the Australian Faunal Directory; IUCN page itself could not be fetched, status relayed via FishBase/Wikipedia.

facts.statement: The Cocos (Keeling) Islands' capital, West Island, sits at roughly 12°11′13″ S, 96°49′42″ E in the eastern Indian Ocean.
facts.evidence_note: Infobox coordinates for West Island.
facts.subject: island

facts.statement: The islands lie about 3,685 km (2,290 mi) west of Darwin and about 900 km southwest of Christmas Island.
facts.evidence_note: Opening summary of the Britannica entry.
facts.subject: island

facts.statement: The group consists of 27 coral islands arranged in two atolls, and only West Island and Home Island have permanent residents.
facts.evidence_note: Geography section; SBS factbox also says 27 islands, 24 of them in South Keeling.
facts.subject: island

facts.statement: North Keeling, a small separate atoll, lies roughly 25 km north of the South Keeling atoll.
facts.evidence_note: Description of the two atolls in the image caption.
facts.subject: island

facts.statement: At Cocos Island Airport, rainfall averages about 1,970 mm per year (records from 1901), peaking in April at about 243 mm and bottoming out in October at about 79 mm.
facts.source_title: Climate statistics for Cocos Island Airport (site 200284)
facts.evidence_note: Rainfall rows of the station averages table.
facts.subject: island

facts.statement: Temperatures are steady: the mean daily maximum is about 29.1 °C and the mean minimum about 24.7 °C, with March warmest (mean max 30.1 °C) and July-August coolest (mean max 28.1 °C).
facts.source_title: Climate statistics for Cocos Island Airport (site 200284)
facts.evidence_note: Temperature rows of the station averages table.
facts.subject: island

facts.statement: Wikipedia classifies the climate as tropical rainforest (Köppen Af) with average annual rainfall of about 1,879 mm, wettest in April and driest in October.
facts.evidence_note: Climate section and climate chart data.
facts.subject: island

facts.statement: The Australian government describes the climate as tropical and very humid, with temperatures of 23-30 °C, about 2,000 mm of rain a year mostly from January to August, and south-east trade winds most of the year.
facts.publisher: Australian Government Dept of Infrastructure, Transport, Regional Development, Communications, Sport and the Arts
facts.evidence_note: Climate paragraph of the environment page.
facts.subject: island

facts.statement: A Ramsar site document notes Australia has warmed about 1.4 °C since 1910 and projects rising temperatures, falling rainfall and rising sea level for the Cocos (Keeling) Islands.
facts.source_title: Ramsar Information Sheet: Pulu Keeling National Park (Site 797)
facts.evidence_note: Climate change section of the Ramsar sheet.
facts.subject: island

facts.statement: Total land area is only about 14.2 km2 with a 26 km coastline, and the highest point is about 5 m above sea level.
facts.evidence_note: Geography infobox figures.
facts.subject: island

facts.statement: The atolls are horseshoe-shaped, with coral-sand beaches on the ocean side and mudflats on the lagoon side.
facts.publisher: Australian Government Dept of Infrastructure, Transport, Regional Development, Communications, Sport and the Arts
facts.evidence_note: Geography paragraph of the environment page.
facts.subject: island

facts.statement: North Keeling is a C-shaped atoll of about 1.2 km2 enclosing a lagoon of about 0.5 km2, whose eastern opening is roughly 50 m wide.
facts.evidence_note: Description in the Area section.
facts.subject: island

facts.statement: The low reef islands rise only 3-4 m above sea level and sit on a platform of cemented coral rock built from corals dated 4000-3000 radiocarbon years before present, with the islands accumulating over about the last 3000 years.
facts.source_title: The Cocos (Keeling) Islands, and what coral reefs can tell us about changes of sea level
facts.evidence_note: Cocos section of the sea-level vignette.
facts.subject: island

facts.statement: Charles Darwin visited in 1836 and developed his theory that atolls form as a sinking volcanic island leaves a coral ring behind; a NASA page says Beagle depth studies supported this idea.
facts.evidence_note: Geology paragraph; SERC page confirms 1836 visit and 1842 publication.
facts.subject: island

facts.statement: William Keeling, a European captain, sighted the islands in 1609.
facts.evidence_note: History paragraph.
facts.subject: island

facts.statement: John Clunies-Ross first visited in 1825 and later settled with his family, who ruled the islands almost like a private fiefdom for nearly 150 years.
facts.evidence_note: History section.
facts.subject: island

facts.statement: HMS Beagle reached the islands on 1 April 1836 with Charles Darwin aboard for survey work.
facts.evidence_note: History section.
facts.subject: island

facts.statement: On 9 November 1914, HMAS Sydney fought the German raider SMS Emden off the islands, and the Emden ended up driven aground on North Keeling.
facts.evidence_note: Battle of Cocos entry; NAA page also says Emden was driven ashore on North Keeling.
facts.subject: island

facts.statement: The islands became an Australian territory on 23 November 1955 under the Cocos (Keeling) Islands Act 1955.
facts.evidence_note: Transfer paragraph; Australian government governance page gives the same date.
facts.subject: island

facts.statement: In a 1984 UN-supervised self-determination vote, 229 of 261 eligible voters chose full integration with Australia.
facts.evidence_note: History section vote tally; government page confirms the vote favoured integration.
facts.subject: island

facts.statement: The islands are an Australian external territory governed under section 122 of the Constitution, with a Minister for Territories, an Administrator appointed by the Governor-General, and Western Australian law applied through the 1955 Act.
facts.publisher: Australian Government Dept of Infrastructure, Transport, Regional Development, Communications, Sport and the Arts
facts.evidence_note: Status and Act summary.
facts.subject: island

facts.statement: The population was 593 at the 2021 Census, mainly Cocos Malay people who mostly speak Malay at home (61.2%) and are mostly Sunni Muslims.
facts.evidence_note: Demographics section.
facts.subject: island

facts.statement: Local services are run by the Shire of Cocos (Keeling) Islands, and residents vote federally in the Northern Territory Division of Lingiari.
facts.publisher: Australian Government Dept of Infrastructure, Transport, Regional Development, Communications, Sport and the Arts
facts.evidence_note: Local government and electoral representation bullets.
facts.subject: island

facts.statement: North Keeling is the only seabird breeding area within 900 km, and about 60 bird species have been recorded across the islands.
facts.publisher: Australian Government Dept of Infrastructure, Transport, Regional Development, Communications, Sport and the Arts
facts.evidence_note: Fauna section.
facts.subject: island

facts.statement: North Keeling regularly supports about 30,000 breeding pairs of red-footed boobies, roughly 6% of the global population.
facts.source_title: Ramsar Information Sheet: Pulu Keeling National Park (Site 797)
facts.evidence_note: Species numbers in the Ramsar sheet.
facts.subject: island

facts.statement: The Cocos buff-banded rail is the islands' only endemic bird; the Ramsar sheet estimates 422-711 birds on North Keeling and notes a 2013 reintroduction to Horsburgh Island.
facts.source_title: Ramsar Information Sheet: Pulu Keeling National Park (Site 797)
facts.evidence_note: Rail section of the Ramsar sheet.
facts.subject: island

facts.statement: Sixty-one plant species have been recorded in the territory, with one endemic subspecies, Pandanus tectorius cocosensis, found on Home and West Islands.
facts.publisher: Australian Government Dept of Infrastructure, Transport, Regional Development, Communications, Sport and the Arts
facts.evidence_note: Flora section.
facts.subject: island

facts.statement: The marine park region has over 600 reef fish species and a genetically distinct local green turtle stock.
facts.evidence_note: Species section of the marine park page.
facts.subject: island

facts.statement: Sea level is projected to rise about 14-17 cm by 2030 and 40-50 cm by 2070 at the national park, on islands only a few metres high.
facts.source_title: Pulu Keeling National Park climate change strategy
facts.publisher: Australian Government Dept of Agriculture, Fisheries and Forestry
facts.evidence_note: Sea level rise projections in the climate strategy.
facts.subject: island

facts.statement: Cyclone John in 1989 killed about 40% of booby chicks and 2% of adults, cut nest numbers by 60% the following year, and the colony recovered after four years.
facts.source_title: Pulu Keeling National Park climate change strategy
facts.publisher: Australian Government Dept of Agriculture, Fisheries and Forestry
facts.evidence_note: Red-footed booby passage in the strategy.
facts.subject: island

facts.statement: Yellow crazy ants were detected across 59 ha of North Keeling in 2009, and illegal seabird poaching was estimated at 2,000-3,000 birds a year in 2004.
facts.source_title: Ramsar Information Sheet: Pulu Keeling National Park (Site 797)
facts.evidence_note: Threats section of the Ramsar sheet.
facts.subject: island

facts.statement: Pulu Keeling National Park was established on 12 December 1995 and listed as Ramsar Site 797 on 17 March 1996, with legal hunting having ended in 1989.
facts.evidence_note: Conservation section; Ramsar site page confirms 17 March 1996 and 2,603 ha.
facts.subject: island

facts.statement: The Cocos (Keeling) Islands Marine Park was proclaimed on 20 March 2022 and extends out to the edge of Australia's EEZ, covering roughly 467,000 km2.
facts.evidence_note: Establishment and size sections; page lists 467,054 and 467,754 km2.
facts.subject: island

facts.statement: GBIF holds 24 occurrence records of Cheilinus undulatus from the Cocos (Keeling) Islands, including recent human observations.
facts.source_title: GBIF occurrence search: Cheilinus undulatus in Cocos (Keeling) Islands
facts.evidence_note: Occurrence search count and records.
facts.subject: napoleon-wrasse

facts.statement: The Australian Faunal Directory lists the humphead (giant) wrasse as occurring at Christmas Island and the Cocos (Keeling) Islands.
facts.evidence_note: Distribution section citing Hobbs et al. 2014.
facts.subject: napoleon-wrasse

facts.statement: FishBase reports the species as Endangered (criteria A2bcd) on the IUCN Red List, assessed 17 July 2024.
facts.evidence_note: Conservation status line.
facts.subject: napoleon-wrasse

facts.statement: Wikipedia attributes the Endangered status to a 2004 IUCN assessment, which differs from the 2024 date shown by FishBase.
facts.evidence_note: Conservation status citation.
facts.subject: napoleon-wrasse

facts.statement: Males can reach about 229 cm and 191 kg, while females rarely exceed 1 m.
facts.evidence_note: Description section; FishBase gives a similar 229 cm maximum.
facts.subject: napoleon-wrasse

facts.statement: The species is a female-to-male sex changer that matures at 5-7 years and lives about 30 years.
facts.evidence_note: Biology section.
facts.subject: napoleon-wrasse

facts.statement: Its main threat is overfishing for the live reef food-fish trade, and it is listed in CITES Appendix II.
facts.evidence_note: Threats and CITES lines.
facts.subject: napoleon-wrasse

facts.statement: The Ramsar sheet for Pulu Keeling National Park (North Keeling) lists the green turtle (Chelonia mydas) as EN, i.e. endangered, on the IUCN Red List, records it nesting on the park's sandy beaches, and also notes it is vulnerable under Australia's EPBC Act.
facts.source_title: Ramsar Information Sheet: Pulu Keeling National Park (Site 797)
facts.evidence_note: Section 3.3 species table (EN) and Section 3.1 text. IUCN category is relayed by the Ramsar sheet; the Red List page itself was not fetched.
facts.subject: island

facts.statement: The Ramsar sheet lists the hawksbill turtle (Eretmochelys imbricata) as CR, critically endangered, on the IUCN Red List and says it forages in the park's waters, with nesting there not recorded; the sheet also notes EPBC vulnerable status.
facts.source_title: Ramsar Information Sheet: Pulu Keeling National Park (Site 797)
facts.evidence_note: Section 3.3 species table (CR) and Section 3.1. IUCN category relayed by the Ramsar sheet, not checked on the Red List itself.
facts.subject: island

facts.statement: A 2006 (Year 7) sea turtle project report for Parks Australia gave preliminary mean population estimates, pooled across all survey years, of about 406 hawksbill turtles in the West Island catch area and about 410 in the South Island catch area, but said mark-recapture was not yielding enough green turtle recaptures to estimate population size.
facts.source_title: Green and hawksbill turtles at Cocos (Keeling), 2006 (Year 7 report)
facts.publisher: Australian Government Dept of Agriculture, Fisheries and Forestry
facts.evidence_note: Foraging population results, 2006 (Year 7) report. Local capture-recapture estimates for study areas only, not a whole-territory count; the report's capture total is internally inconsistent (261 in text vs 245 in a table). Statement corrected after an independent re-read of the source.
facts.subject: island

facts.statement: The robber crab (Birgus latro), the large land crab also called the coconut crab, is listed as VU, vulnerable, in the Ramsar sheet for Pulu Keeling National Park, which flags it as an internationally listed threatened species present on North Keeling.
facts.source_title: Ramsar Information Sheet: Pulu Keeling National Park (Site 797)
facts.evidence_note: Section 3.3 species table (VU) and Section 3.1. Population size is not stated. IUCN category relayed by the Ramsar sheet.
facts.subject: island

facts.statement: The yellowhead angelfish (Centropyge joculator) is found in the eastern Indian Ocean at the Cocos and Christmas Islands and is listed as Least Concern by the IUCN per FishBase, assessed 09 October 2009.
facts.evidence_note: Distribution and IUCN fields on the FishBase summary page; habitat given as coral and rubble on steep outer reef slopes at 8-70 m depth, max length 9 cm. The Ramsar sheet separately calls it endemic to Christmas and Cocos (Keeling). Statement corrected after an independent re-read of the source.
facts.subject: island

facts.statement: The Cocos buff-banded rail (Gallirallus philippensis andrewsi), the islands' endemic rail subspecies, is described by Wikipedia as endangered under Australia's EPBC Act, with an estimated 850-1,000 birds at 7-8 per hectare, now effectively confined to North Keeling after disappearing from most of the southern atoll.
facts.evidence_note: Conservation status, population, habitat and extinction sections. The page gives no IUCN Red List status. Population figures differ from the Ramsar sheet (422-711 birds in text, 1,000 in a table), which is already noted among the file's conflicts.
facts.subject: island

facts.statement: The lesser frigatebird (Fregata ariel) is listed as LC by the Ramsar sheet for Pulu Keeling National Park, which gives 6,000 individuals (3,000 pairs) from a 2004 count, about 3% of the global population, breeding in large numbers on North Keeling.
facts.source_title: Ramsar Information Sheet: Pulu Keeling National Park (Site 797)
facts.evidence_note: Section 3.3 animal species table. Units differ (individuals vs pairs) between table columns; figures are as stated by the sheet.
facts.subject: island

facts.statement: A 2014 hard-coral survey paper (Richards and Hobbs), citing Veron (1994), says two reef corals, Anacropora forbesi and Montipora spumosa, may be extinct at the Cocos (Keeling) Islands; Cocos is the type locality for Anacropora forbesi.
facts.source_title: The status of hard coral diversity at Christmas Island and Cocos (Keeling) Islands
facts.publisher: Raffles Bulletin of Zoology (Lee Kong Chian Natural History Museum, NUS)
facts.evidence_note: Cocos comparison section (p. 384). Wording is 'may be extinct', not a confirmed extinction. The same paper counts 99 scleractinian species for Cocos from Veron (1994). Statement corrected after an independent re-read of the source.
facts.subject: island

facts.statement: A study in Scientific Reports estimated that the Cocos (Keeling) Islands hold roughly 414 million pieces of anthropogenic debris weighing about 238 tonnes, extrapolated from sampling 7 of the 27 islands in 2017 (88% of the group's landmass).
facts.source_title: Scientific Reports (2019) article on anthropogenic debris on the Cocos (Keeling) Islands
facts.evidence_note: Abstract and methods. The raw survey counted 23,227 items weighing 96.67 kg on 1,110 m2 of beach; the authors call the totals minimum estimates.
facts.subject: island

facts.statement: About 93% of the estimated debris on the Cocos (Keeling) Islands (around 383 million items) is buried up to 10 cm deep in the sand, about 60% of that buried debris is micro-debris of 2-5 mm, and plastic made up 95.41% of recorded items.
facts.source_title: Scientific Reports (2019) article on anthropogenic debris on the Cocos (Keeling) Islands
facts.evidence_note: Abstract and results. Debris deeper than 10 cm was not counted, and some hotspots could not be reached.
facts.subject: island

facts.statement: Geoscience Australia describes a freshwater lens beneath Home Island in the Cocos (Keeling) Islands that is theoretically up to 19 m thick (about 15 m on average) over roughly 30 hectares, with an estimated sustainable yield of about 200,000 litres per day.
facts.source_title: The freshwater lens on Home Island in the Cocos (Keeling) Islands
facts.evidence_note: Dataset description. Recommended pumping should lower lens thickness by no more than half to avoid saltwater contamination. The reference date is 2018; the record itself was created in 2025.
facts.subject: island

facts.statement: The Australian Government has contracted a new 200 kilolitre-per-day seawater reverse osmosis (SWRO) plant on West Island, Cocos (Keeling) Islands, which will replace the freshwater lens below the operational airfield, after a water source beach bore drilling program was completed in November 2022.
facts.source_title: Fact Sheet 1, March 2023: West Island seawater reverse osmosis desalination plant
facts.publisher: Australian Government Dept of Infrastructure, Transport, Regional Development, Communications and the Arts
facts.evidence_note: Fact Sheet 1, March 2023. This is a planned project as of that date; construction status was not confirmed. Water Corporation has run water services on the islands since 2001. Statement corrected after an independent re-read of the source.
facts.subject: island

facts.statement: In the Cocos (Keeling) Islands Marine Park, offshore waters from about 3 nautical miles out to the Exclusive Economic Zone limit are a green (National Park) zone closed to fishing and mining, while most inshore waters are a yellow (Habitat Protection) zone where fishing is allowed.
facts.evidence_note: Zones section. Two small inshore green zones also exist, at the Rip on Direction Island and Trannies Beach on West Island. The page's park area figures conflict (467,054 vs 467,754 km2).
facts.subject: island

facts.statement: The lagoon of North Keeling is at most 2 m deep, and since 2005 natural deposits have closed its former ocean entrance so that seawater no longer flows into it.
facts.evidence_note: Lagoon section of the Pulu Keeling National Park geology page.
facts.subject: island

facts.statement: After the lagoon entrance at North Keeling closed in 2005, the Ramsar sheet says seagrass (Thalassia hemprichii) was lost and replaced by cyanobacteria mats, and that without flushing the lagoon may become deoxygenated and brackish.
facts.source_title: Ramsar Information Sheet: Pulu Keeling National Park (Site 797)
facts.evidence_note: Sections 2.2.1, 4.3.1 and 4.3.2. The sheet is inconsistent on salinity (30-40 g/l in 4.4.7 but 'brackish' in 4.4.9) and notes pH and nutrients are unknown.
facts.subject: island

facts.statement: A literature review in the Western Australian CHRMAP appendices says sea surface temperature at the Cocos (Keeling) Islands has increased by about 0.5 degrees C, with stronger warming in winter.
facts.evidence_note: Literature review on climate trends (p. 246). Secondary summary of earlier studies; the underlying study and period for the sea temperature trend are not given on the page read.
facts.subject: island

facts.statement: At Cocos Island Airport, mean 9 am wind speed averages 25.6 km/h over the year, lowest in February (18.2 km/h) and highest in September (30.6 km/h), matching the strong south-east trade winds of the drier months.
facts.source_title: Climate statistics for Cocos Island Airport (site 200284)
facts.evidence_note: Wind speed table, records 1952-2014. The link to trade winds is an interpretation consistent with the Australian Government description, not stated in the table.
facts.subject: island

facts.statement: The Ramsar sheet classifies the climate as tropical humid monsoonal (Am), with annual rainfall ranging from 855 to 3,490 mm and averaging 1,979 mm, a north-west monsoon from January to May and south-east trade winds for much of the year.
facts.source_title: Ramsar Information Sheet: Pulu Keeling National Park (Site 797)
facts.evidence_note: Sections 2.2.1 and 4.4.1. Wikipedia classifies the climate as Af instead; the averaging periods differ between sources.
facts.subject: island

facts.statement: The Pulu Keeling climate strategy (citing Maunsell 2009) says the number of tropical cyclones within 500 km of the islands will decrease by 25 per cent, but the frequency of high-intensity cyclones (category 4 or 5) is projected to double.
facts.source_title: Pulu Keeling National Park climate change strategy
facts.publisher: Australian Government Dept of Agriculture, Fisheries and Forestry
facts.evidence_note: Section 3, Biodiversity impacts. These are model projections cited by the strategy, not observations. Statement corrected after an independent re-read of the source.
facts.subject: island

facts.statement: Severe Tropical Cyclone Walter passed about 130 km north of the Cocos Islands as it moved southwest, gales were reported there, and the Bureau of Meteorology notes no known damage.
facts.evidence_note: Bureau cyclone history page for Walter. The year and wind speeds at Cocos are not given in the page summary read.
facts.subject: island

facts.statement: The CHRMAP appendices cite an observed sea-level rise of about 4 mm per year at the Cocos (Keeling) Islands since 1992 and adopt planning allowances of 0.4 m over 50 years and 0.9 m over 100 years.
facts.evidence_note: Literature review (p. 246) for the observed rate, attributed to Maunsell-AECOM (2009); planning values from p. 249 under SPP 2.6.
facts.subject: island

facts.statement: A study of southeast Indian Ocean reefs says the Cocos (Keeling) Islands have positive sea-surface temperature anomalies in early summer during La Nina, which makes the reef susceptible to coral bleaching during both phases of ENSO.
facts.source_title: Opposite polarities of ENSO drive distinct patterns of coral bleaching potentials in the southeast Indian Ocean
facts.evidence_note: Introduction and results. The paper gives no Cocos-specific temperature magnitudes or bleaching percentages.
facts.subject: island

facts.statement: Pulu Keeling National Park records 40 plant species, including several not found on the southern Cocos islands, in four main vegetation types: pisonia forest, octopus bush shrubland, tea shrub and ironwood thickets, and open grassy areas.
facts.evidence_note: Species counts section. The page says pisonia forest dominates and is nesting habitat for tens of thousands of red-footed boobies. The territory-wide figure of 61 plant species is in an earlier fact and is a different scope.
facts.subject: island

facts.statement: Parks Australia reports 201 fish species recorded in Pulu Keeling National Park waters, and because the Cocos (Keeling) Islands lie within the ranges of both Indian and Pacific Ocean fish, there is a large number of hybrid fish.
facts.source_title: Pulu Keeling National Park: Marine life
facts.evidence_note: Marine life page. The page says many more species remain unsurveyed; the marine park elsewhere cites over 600 reef fish for the wider region. Statement corrected after an independent re-read of the source.
facts.subject: island

facts.statement: At least 26 land- and water-dwelling crab species live in Pulu Keeling National Park, including three abundant hermit crabs (Coenobita perlatus, C. brevimanus, C. rugosus) and the Christmas Island red crab (Gecarcoidea natalis).
facts.evidence_note: Crabs page. No conservation status or counts are given there; abundance is described only as common or in large numbers.
facts.subject: island

facts.statement: Yellow crazy ants have been found in the pisonia forests of North Keeling and are associated with scale insects that can kill pisonia canopies, which have not been detected in the park, while six exotic plant species occur there but none is currently a severe problem.
facts.evidence_note: Conservation page, Threats, Yellow crazy ants and Weed control sections.
facts.subject: island
